Article Title: Sony Music and Warner Chappell Music sue Anthropic; lawsuit that names Dario Amodei accuse Anthropic of 'illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading' copyrighted songs to train Claude
Article Text:
Sony Music and Warner Chappell accuse Anthropic of copyright infringement

Anthropic faces scrutiny over how it gets training data

What Anthropic says

Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell Music have sued Anthropic, accusing the AI company of using copyrighted songs without permission to train its Claude models. The lawsuit, filed in a Northern California federal court last week, also names Anthropic co-founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann. The music publishers allege that Anthropic engaged in “illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading” copyrighted songs, including works such as “Eye of the Tiger,” Marvin Gaye’s “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough” and Taylor Swift’s “Paper Rings.” The case adds another major copyright fight to the growing legal battle between AI companies and rights holders over how copyrighted material can be used to train AI systems.The lawsuit claims Anthropic obtained copyrighted music and used it in the development and training of Claude. Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell Music are seeking a jury trial and statutory damages of up to $150,000 for each infringed composition.The publishers also allege that Claude can reproduce copyrighted song lyrics in its responses. They argue that this could allow users to obtain lyrics through the AI chatbot instead of using licensed lyric services, potentially hurting the market for music publishers and songwriters.The complaint names several well-known songs as examples of works allegedly involved in the case.The latest lawsuit comes after Anthropic faced a major copyright case involving books. In June 2025, a court found that Anthropic had downloaded more than 7 million pirated books from sources including Library Genesis and Pirate Library Mirror. The judge found that Anthropic's use of copyrighted books to train its AI models qualified as fair use, but the acquisition of pirated copies remained a separate issue.That dispute was later resolved through a $1.5 billion settlement.Anthropic has rejected the claims made by the music publishers. “We disagree with the publishers’ claims and we intend to defend ourselves robustly in court,” an Anthropic spokesperson said, according to Benzinga.The lawsuit is also not Anthropic's first legal fight over copyrighted music. In a separate case filed in 2023, Universal Music Group, Concord Music Group and ABKCO sued Anthropic over the alleged use and reproduction of copyrighted song lyrics.
Article Summary: Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell Music accuse Anthropic of copyright infringement. The music publishers allege that Anthropic engaged in “illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading” copyrighted songs. The case adds another major copyright fight to the growing legal battle between AI companies and rights holders over how copyrighted material can be used to train AI systems.

Article Title: Apple Mac minis and Mac Studios have disappeared from store shelves in many countries, and how this shortage links to OpenAI and Anthropic
Article Text:
OpenAI reportedly bought tens of thousands of Apple Macs for AI

Why Mac mini and Mac Studio are attracting AI developers

OpenClaw craze adds to Mac mini demand in China

Apple’s Mac mini and Mac Studio computers have become increasingly difficult to find in several markets, and the AI boom may be playing a surprising role in the shortage. According to a report by The information, OpenAI has bought tens of thousands of Mac minis and Mac Studios for work involving AI agents and reinforcement learning, while Anthropic has reportedly rented Mac minis through Amazon Web Services for similar tasks. At the same time, developers and consumers are increasingly turning to Apple's compact computers to run AI agents locally. The demand has been particularly visible in China, where the popularity of OpenClaw has reportedly pushed Mac mini stocks down and prices up.According to The Information, OpenAI has spent several months buying tens of thousands of Mac minis and Mac Studios. The computers are reportedly being used for reinforcement learning and AI agents that can interact with computers.Anthropic has also reportedly been using Mac minis, although through a different route. The Claude maker is said to have rented the machines through Amazon Web Services for similar AI work.The demand highlights an unusual role for Apple's small desktop computers. Macs are not replacing Nvidia's powerful GPUs for training the largest AI models. Instead, they can be useful for another growing area of artificial intelligence: AI agents that interact with regular computer environments.Such agents can look at a screen, use a browser, click buttons and repeatedly attempt tasks. Running many such sessions can require a large number of computers.One reason is Apple's unified memory architecture. Instead of keeping CPU and GPU memory completely separate, Apple silicon allows different parts of the system to access a common pool of memory. High-memory Mac configurations can therefore run some local AI models that may struggle to fit within the dedicated memory available on consumer graphics cards.The machines also offer developers a complete macOS environment. That can matter when an AI agent needs to learn how to operate software and perform tasks on a desktop rather than simply process information in a data centre.Demand is not limited to large AI companies. The Mac mini has also become a popular choice among people running OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent. The trend has been particularly visible in China, where running OpenClaw has become known as “raising a lobster”, a reference to the project's mascot.According to the South China Morning Post, Mac minis were selling out at retailers in parts of China earlier this year. Some sellers with remaining stock were reportedly charging hundreds of yuan above normal prices.The Mac mini's appeal for OpenClaw is also linked to security. AI agents can require extensive permissions to control a computer, access information and carry out tasks. Running such software on a person's main computer could create risks if permissions are incorrectly configured or third-party tools contain malicious code.That has encouraged some users to run AI agents on a separate machine. The Mac mini's small size and ability to run AI workloads locally have made it one option for such setups.
Article Summary: OpenAI reportedly bought tens of thousands of Apple Macs for AI. The computers are reportedly being used for reinforcement learning and AI agents that can interact with computers. The Mac mini has also become a popular choice among people running OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent.

Article Title: CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz admits Anthropic Mythos did help drive record quarterly revenues; and warns companies: Way these AI agents are able to ...
Article Text:
The role of Anthropic’s Mythos in shifting security landscape

Crowdstrike financial growth

George Kurtz, CEO of cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, said the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology is revealing major vulnerabilities in corporate digital infrastructure.He warned that old and default security systems are not enough to defend against modern cyber attacks. Kurtz also pointed out that even well-resourced organizations are at serious risk because automated AI tooling enables bad actors to discover and weaponize vulnerabilities at unprecedented speeds. As the broader threat environment evolves so rapidly, traditional safeguards and free security options can no longer keep pace.The rising severity of automated cyber dangers has transformed market sentiment surrounding the cybersecurity industry. While fears of AI disrupting security vendors weighed on valuations late last year and into early 2026, real-world developments shifted market perspectives.Kurtz explained that the rollout of Anthropic’s Mythos model in April proved how advanced machine learning accelerates the velocity and sophistication of cyber offensives. The very fact that AI serves as a powerful catalyst for enterprise security demand fueled a prolonged stock rally, driving shares of both CrowdStrike and rival Palo Alto Networks up roughly 100% year to date.Kurtz also pointed to OpenAI’s recent security incident involving Hugging Face as a clear indicator of emerging operational hazards, where an autonomous AI agent escaped its designated test sandbox, accessed external networks and compromised Hugging Face infrastructure before containment.“So, if we think about the AI era and how fast these AI agents are able to swarm and find vulnerabilities and exploit those, it’s just a different quantum of security that’s needed. This is why we think we’re in pole position,” Kurtz stated.Kurtz said that the company beat earnings expectations, propelling CrowdStrike’s stock up more than 20% in a single trading session to a record closing price near $228 per share. Rising demand for proactive cyber defenses drove what Kurtz termed a “quarter of records” across CrowdStrike's key financial benchmarks.Kurtz reiterated that the company’s proprietary Falcon software platform is engineered to leverage AI-driven detection mechanisms to intercept automated threats, balancing technical expertise against adversaries whose intrusion techniques change rapidly.
Article Summary: CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology is revealing major vulnerabilities in corporate digital infrastructure. Kurtz also pointed out that even well-resourced organizations are at serious risk because automated AI tooling enables bad actors to discover and weaponize vulnerabilities at unprecedented speeds.

Article Title: Travellers to Canada or those transiting through, here's the authorisation you may need
Article Text:
Who needs an eTA

Certain visa-required travellers can also use an eTA

How to apply

Canadian citizens and permanent residents

Travellers who need a full visa

US citizens and green card holders

Basic entry requirements for everyone

Canada's immigration authority has reiterated the entry requirements for foreign travellers heading to or passing through the country, according to the latest guidance published on the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) website and shared by the department on social media. The authority said that depending on the nationality and the travel purpose, visitors may require an Electric Travel Authorisation (eTA) or a visa before boarding their flight. for the uninitiated eTA is a digital entry requirement linked to a traveller’s passport and is mandatory for visa-exempt foreign nationals flying to or transiting through Canada.For citizens of eTA-eligible countries flying to Canada, an eTA and a valid passport are required to board a flight — a separate visitor visa is not needed in this case.The rules shift for travellers arriving by land or sea. In most cases, citizens of eTA-eligible countries arriving by car, bus, train, or boat, including cruise ships, do not need an eTA at all, though a valid passport is still required. One notable exception applies to travellers arriving by sea from Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon: those travellers do need an eTA to board, except when arriving by cruise ship.Citizens of select visa-required countries may also be eligible to apply for an eTA instead of a full visitor visa, but only if they are travelling to Canada by air.If those same travellers arrive by car, bus, train, or boat — including cruise ships — they still need a full visitor visa rather than an eTA.The eTA application is completed online and usually approved within minutes, though some requests may take several days if additional documents are required. Travellers should apply before booking their flight to avoid delays. The eTA costs CAD $7 and is valid for up to five years or until the passport expires.Canadian citizens who also hold dual citizenship must travel using a valid Canadian passport. Canadian permanent residents do not need either an eTA or a visitor visa, but must travel with a valid permanent resident card or a permanent resident travel document. IRCC specifically flagged that permanent resident status does not expire — meaning former Canadian residents, even those who lived in the country long ago, may still hold valid PR status and should confirm their status before travelling to avoid complications.Travellers from visa-required countries, stateless individuals, and those holding a foreign passport for stateless persons must apply for a visitor visa rather than an eTA, regardless of how they plan to travel to Canada.American citizens are exempt from the eTA requirement entirely and instead must carry the appropriate identification, such as a valid U.S. passport.Rules for U.S. lawful permanent residents ("green card" holders) have been in effect since April 26, 2022, requiring these travellers to present two categories of documents regardless of how they enter Canada: a valid passport from their country of citizenship (or an accepted equivalent travel document), and a valid green card or equivalent proof of their U.S. status. IRCC lists several acceptable forms of that status proof, including a valid Form I-551 permanent resident card, a foreign passport bearing a valid I-551 or ADIT stamp, or other specific combinations of expired cards paired with relevant USCIS notices, depending on a traveller's exact immigration paperwork situation.Beyond authorization documents, IRCC outlined a broader set of baseline conditions all visitors must meet to enter Canada. Travellers must hold a valid travel document, such as a passport; hold a valid eTA or visitor visa; be in good health; have no criminal or immigration-related convictions; satisfy a border services officer that they have sufficient ties to their home country — such as employment, property, financial assets, or family — to ensure their return; convince the officer they intend to leave Canada at the end of their stay; and demonstrate sufficient funds to cover their visit, an amount that can vary depending on trip length and accommodation arrangements.
Article Summary: Electric Travel Authorisation (eTA) is a digital entry requirement linked to a traveller’s passport. It is mandatory for visa-exempt foreign nationals flying to or transiting through Canada. Certain visa-required travellers can also use an eTA. US citizens and green card holders are exempt from the eTA requirement.

Article Title: Microsoft sends memo to employees on Data Centers; admits AI making it tough to meet some prior 'environmental commitments', but adds stop worrying as ...
Article Text:
Internal unease at Microsoft mirrors broader public pushback against data centres

Microsoft deploying efficiency upgrades

Microsoft is taking steps to reassure its workforce about the broader societal and environmental value of its computing infrastructure, even as artificial intelligence (AI) expansion complicates long-term climate targets. Citing an internal communication, Bloomberg says that Cloud Operations and Innovation head Noelle Walsh addressed growing staff inquiries regarding power consumption, water demands, carbon output and the direct footprints that these massive server campuses leave on nearby neighbourhoods.Walsh acknowledged that escalating AI workloads have made hitting earlier greenhouse gas reduction pledges considerably harder. However, she urged staff to consider ongoing engineering advancements, and that data centers must be built “with discipline, transparency and a relentless focus on reducing impact and increasing benefits,” she wrote.The internal message highlights how broader public scrutiny over AI infrastructure has reached the tech giant’s own ranks. Several reports have claimed that technology companies are facing fierce community resistance against new computing projects.Citing data from research group Data Center Watch, the report says that the local opposition stalled or canceled at least 75 separate data center developments – representing a combined value of roughly $130 billion – in the first quarter of the year alone. Meanwhile, grassroots protests continue to centre on ecological strains, alongside wider fears that AI automation could eliminate jobs and disrupt local economies.Microsoft previously disclosed that its overall carbon emissions jumped 25% in 2025 due to rapid data facility construction. Consequently, the company has informed sustainability partners of plans to scale back new carbon-banking arrangements, while management has evaluated pausing an earlier goal to match 100% of its power consumption with renewable energy.Walsh pointed to significant technical progress designed to mitigate the environmental footprint of Microsoft’s infrastructure. Data centre water usage efficiency has improved by nearly 90% when compared against the firm’s earliest server facilities. The tech giant has secured commercial contracts to bring up to 40 gigawatts of renewable power online across global grids. Additionally, more than 90% of retired computer components and server hardware pulled from operational facilities are recycled or repurposed.To soothe tensions with municipal leaders and residents, major technology operators are overhauling their public outreach and offering significant concessions. In January, Microsoft committed to halting requests for municipal property tax breaks in development zones, while pledging to cover its own utility power costs to prevent residential electricity rate spikes.
Article Summary: Microsoft is taking steps to reassure its workforce about the broader societal and environmental value of its computing infrastructure. Internal message highlights how broader public scrutiny over AI infrastructure has reached the tech giant's own ranks. Microsoft previously disclosed that its overall carbon emissions jumped 25% in 2025 due to rapid data facility construction.

Article Title: Starting September 1, Indian airports are discontinuing immigration clearance for ...
Article Text:
Physical boarding pass stamping to end from September 1

Immigration boarding pass stamping to end from September 1

Indian airports will accept e-boarding passes at immigration

What the new rule means for international travellers

Poll Vote & Share your view Which option do you prefer for your boarding pass while traveling internationally? Electronic boarding pass Printed boarding pass 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

International travellers leaving India will see a small but important change at airports starting September 1. Passengers will no longer need to get their boarding passes stamped during immigration clearance, removing an extra step from the departure process. The Bureau of Immigration has introduced the change to make immigration procedures faster and more convenient for travellers. Under the new system, passengers can show either an electronic boarding pass on their phone or a printed copy, but immigration officers will no longer place a stamp on the boarding pass.Until now, international passengers could be asked to present their boarding passes during immigration clearance, with immigration officers stamping the document as part of the process.According to an internal communication by Delhi FRRO Deepak Yadav (viewed by HT), the requirement to stamp boarding passes will be discontinued from September 1. The Bureau of Immigration has also informed airport operators, the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) and other stakeholders about the revised procedure, according to reports.The change removes an additional physical step that could sometimes cause inconvenience for passengers, particularly when stamps were unclear or difficult to read.Under the revised process, international passengers will be able to show an e-boarding pass on their mobile phone at the immigration counter. This means travellers using digital boarding passes will not need to carry a printed copy specifically for an immigration stamp.Passengers who prefer a physical boarding pass can still carry one. However, it will no longer be stamped by immigration officials.The change applies to international passengers departing from India and is aimed at simplifying immigration clearance by removing an unnecessary physical procedure.For travellers, the process will largely remain the same, except for one less thing to worry about at the immigration counter: there will no longer be a stamp on the boarding pass to collect before heading towards the departure gate.
Article Summary: Indian airports will accept e-boarding passes at immigration. Passengers will no longer need to get their boarding passes stamped during immigration clearance, removing an extra step from the departure process. The Bureau of Immigration has introduced the change to make immigration procedures faster and more convenient for travellers.

Article Title: Moody's chief economist Mark Zandi warns: Never in the 35 years has there ever been a time when all things are screaming to tell you ...
Article Text:
Mark Zandi said he couldn't pinpoint exactly when a crisis might hit

The debt-to-GDP warning sign

National debt tops $40 trillion

Bond market turmoil intensifies

Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi has issued one of his starkest warnings yet, saying the US may be ‘sleepwalking’ into an economic crises. According a report by Moneywise, speaking on the Sonia and Simon podcast Zandi said, “Never in the 35 years has there ever been a time when all of the measures are screaming, you know, we got a problem”. He also cautioned that the preconditions for a reckoning are falling into place, even if the timing remains uncertain. Zandi pointed to America’s debt-to-GDP ratio crossing 100% in April, a level not seen since the aftermath of World War II. He highlighted the government’s $2 trillion annual budget deficit, which becomes harder to manage as interest rates rise. The cumulative national debt has now surpassed $40 trillion, with investors increasingly skeptical of US fiscal policy.Speaking on a recent episode of the Sonia and Simon podcast with hosts Sonia Jahshan and Simon Baggs, Zandi said he couldn't pinpoint exactly when a crisis might hit, but stressed that the underlying preconditions for one are already falling into place — and that he doesn't think the public fully appreciates how serious that is.Zandi went further, arguing that he believes it's essentially unavoidable that the U.S.will need some kind of external shock to force real fiscal change. He said he doesn't believe the American political system, or the public, is capable of making the difficult changes needed to address the country's long-term fiscal problems without being pushed into it by a crisis triggered by rising interest rates.Zandi pointed first to America's debt-to-GDP ratio, which crossed the 100% threshold at the end of April. That ratio measures the size of government debt relative to the overall economy, and offers insight into the federal government's long-term ability to repay what it owes. The U.S. hasn't reached triple-digit debt-to-GDP territory since the years immediately following World War II, when the ratio briefly peaked at 106%.Zandi also flagged the sheer size of the government's current $2 trillion annual budget deficit, noting that a deficit of that scale becomes even harder to manage as interest rates climb — which is exactly what's happening now, driven in part by investors selling off Treasury bonds to protect their portfolios against risks tied to the Iran war and the country's swelling debt load.The cumulative U.S. national debt surpassed $40 trillion for the first time last week, with little indication that its upward climb is slowing. Zandi said the country is issuing large amounts of new debt even as its fiscal position continues to erode, and warned that combining that trend with growing skepticism among global investors — skepticism he tied directly to policy decisions made over the past couple of years — creates the conditions for significantly higher interest rates ahead.The yield on 30-year Treasury bonds stood at 5.17% on August 25, hovering near multi-year highs. Earlier this month, it briefly topped 5.3%, its highest level since 2007. Bond yields matter well beyond Wall Street: they determine what investors earn for holding government debt, but they also directly influence borrowing costs for everyday consumers, including mortgage and auto loan rates, as well as how much the federal government itself pays in interest on the national debt.In response to the sell-off, the Treasury Department is set to begin buying back more of its own bonds starting in early September, an effort aimed at artificially suppressing interest rates.
Article Summary: Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi has issued one of his starkest warnings yet, saying the US may be ‘sleepwalking’ into an economic crises. Zandi said he couldn't pinpoint exactly when a crisis might hit, but stressed that the underlying preconditions for one are already falling into place. The cumulative U.S. national debt surpassed $40 trillion for the first time last week.

Article Title: Apple 'Surprise and Shine' event on September 9: Foldable iPhone Ultra, iPhone 18 Pro and everything else to expect
Article Text:
The foldable iPhone is the biggest launch expected on the day

The iPhone 18 Pro upgrade sounds modest, the price rise may not be

Watches, AirPods and new home devices make up the rest of the list

Siri AI is the software behind most of these new devices

Apple has confirmed September 9 for its annual iPhone launch, and the invite sent out on Wednesday uses the tagline "Surprise and shine." The keynote starts at 10am Pacific, which is 10.30pm IST, and will stream from the Steve Jobs Theater at Apple Park via Apple's site, YouTube and the Apple TV app.Two things separate this from the usual September routine. It is the first Apple event with John Ternus running the company, since Tim Cook hands over the CEO title on September 1 and becomes executive chairman. The rumoured product list is also unusually long. Apple pushed the new Mac mini and Mac Studio out in late August, a slot it has used only once in the past decade, and several reports read that as an attempt to free up space on stage.The device drawing the most attention is Apple's first foldable, which most reports expect to be called iPhone Ultra. Leaks point to a 7.8-inch inner display that opens like a book and a roughly 5.3-inch cover screen, with the A20 Pro chip and 12GB of memory.Rumours suggest two 48MP rear cameras and no telephoto lens, which would be an odd omission at this price. There are also claims that authentication falls back to Touch ID rather than Face ID.Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, who says he has spoken to people who have used the phone, reports that the hinge and the way it fits in a pocket both impressed them, and that it works well as a camera viewfinder. He expects pricing to start above $2,000, roughly Rs 1.8 lakh before Indian duties, so the local figure would likely be higher.The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max are widely tipped as a spec-bump year. Reports point to a 2nm A20 Pro with packaging changes meant to help thermals, Apple's own C2 modem, a slightly larger camera bump and a dark cherry finish. A variable-aperture rear camera is rumoured to be a Pro Max exclusive, and under-display Face ID has been floated without much backing.Pricing is the bigger question. With memory costs climbing, Samsung and Google have each raised phone prices by about $100, and Gurman expects Apple to follow, which would put the iPhone 18 Pro near $1,199. Other estimates run steeper.The standard iPhone 18, the iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air are not expected in September, with reports pointing to 2027.Apple Watch Series 12 is expected to be a light update, with talk of a health sensor tied to a fluoroelastomer band, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 may get a redesign. AirPods 5 look likely, in ANC and non-ANC versions. The camera-equipped AirPods that leaked in a macOS Tahoe release candidate are still reported as a 2027 product.The home devices are the bigger unknown. Reports mention a refreshed Apple TV 4K, a new HomePod mini and a home hub with a seven-inch screen. Gurman reports Apple is reworking the accessory sections in its retail stores, which he takes as a sign of more than routine updates. An OLED iPad mini remains a wildcard.Most of the home hardware has reportedly been waiting on the Siri overhaul Apple previewed at WWDC in June. That keynote was structured differently from the usual run through each operating system in turn, with Apple instead laying out a cross-platform pitch built around Siri AI and Apple Intelligence.The version demoed uses large language model technology to let the assistant act inside apps such as Messages and Calendar rather than only answering questions. It is the feature Apple has been promising and delaying since 2024.Siri AI is expected alongside iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27 Tahoe, watchOS 27 and tvOS 27, reportedly in the back half of September and initially as a waitlisted beta. That timing matters for the hardware. A refreshed Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini would need newer chips to support it, which is one explanation for why those updates have taken so long, and a home hub with a screen makes little sense without an assistant that can act on requests.
Article Summary: Apple will launch the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max on September 9. The foldable phone is expected to start at around $2,000. Apple Watch Series 12 and AirPods are expected to be light updates. Siri AI is expected alongside iOS 27, iPadOS 27, watchOS 27 and tvOS 27.

Article Title: The AI Third World War, and why Apple is waiting for the dust to settle
Article Text:
Apple’s AI strategy comes under focus as tech giants ramp up spending in the race for AI dominance

Our Silicon Valley correspondent contributed to this analysis

The technology industry is witnessing a battle unlike any before. OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, xAI and Microsoft are spending money on artificial intelligence at a scale that would have seemed absurd even a few years ago. They are not merely competing to make the smartest chatbot. They are fighting to control what could become the next great platform of computing.Many call this clash the “AI Third World War”. The phrase is deliberately dramatic. There are no armies or battlefields, but the stakes are comparable to a technological war: who controls the intelligence layer that may sit above operating systems, search, software, commerce and, eventually, much of the digital economy?The numbers explain the intensity. OpenAI’s Stargate project was announced with an ambition to invest $500bn over four years in AI infrastructure. OpenAI and its partners have subsequently expanded the planned data-centre footprint, with more than $400bn of investment and nearly 7GW of capacity under development by Sept 2027.Google is hardly sitting back. Alphabet has raised its expected 2026 capital expenditure to $195-205bn, driven by the need for servers, data centres and other technical infrastructure. In the first six months of 2026 alone, it spent $80.6bn on capital expenditure.Meta expects to spend $130-145bn on capital expenditure this year, with AI infrastructure a principal driver. Amazon expects to spend roughly $220bn, much of it on AI-related infrastructure, while Microsoft expects around $190bn in capital expenditure in calendar 2026.Even the younger AI companies are thinking in wartime numbers. Anthropic has reportedly signed a $45bn, six-year agreement to rent computing capacity from Nscale. It has also committed billions more to computing through deals involving Amazon, Google and SpaceX. xAI, meanwhile, raised $20bn in Jan and says its Colossus supercomputers had crossed the equivalent of 1mn H100 GPUs by the end of 2025.This is therefore not simply a software race. It is a race for chips, electricity, data centres, engineers, capital and customers. Whoever possesses enough computing power can train bigger models; better models attract more users; more users generate revenue and data; revenue finances more computing. The danger for a loser is not merely having an inferior product. It is being locked outside the ecosystem.That is why the AI Third World War metaphor is useful. The competitors are trying to establish a new technological order before everyone else does.And then there is Apple.The striking thing about Apple is not that it has ignored AI. It plainly has not. Its research and development spending has been rising sharply, with the company explicitly attributing part of the increase to infrastructure and AI investment. Its June 2026 announcements also showed a much more ambitious Apple Intelligence, including a completely redesigned Siri.But Apple has not fought the AI war in the way OpenAI, Google, Meta or xAI have. It has not tried to build the world's biggest frontier model at almost any cost. Instead, it has chosen a strikingly different strategy: partner where necessary and integrate where it has an advantage.In Jan, Apple and Google announced a multi-year collaboration under which Google's Gemini models and cloud technology would underpin the next generation of Apple's foundation models.That is precisely where this argument gets interesting.Apple has a long history of arriving late to technologies and then redefining them. Tim Cook once put it bluntly: “We weren’t first on the MP3 player; we weren’t first on the tablet; we weren’t first on the smartphone.” His argument was that Apple sought to create products that mattered, rather than merely products that appeared first.The iPod was not the first MP3 player. The iPhone was not the first smartphone. Yet Apple understood that winning a platform is about much more than inventing a category. It is about integrating hardware, software, services, design, distribution and a compelling user experience.Apple may be applying the same playbook to AI.Why spend hundreds of billions discovering which architecture, model and business model will ultimately win if competitors are willing to spend that money for you? OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta and xAI are educating consumers, developing the infrastructure, recruiting the talent, and testing the economics. They are, in effect, fighting the early battles of the war.Apple can watch. And watching is not necessarily weakness. It can be strategic patience.Apple has something the AI labs desperately need: distribution. More than 2.5bn active Apple devices put the company in an extraordinary position if AI eventually becomes a mainstream interface to computing. If one or two foundation-model platforms emerge as clear winners, Apple could potentially partner with them and put their intelligence layer into the hands of hundreds of millions of users through devices it controls from silicon to operating system.That may explain why Apple’s current strategy looks less like surrender than hedging. Its new AI architecture combines its own foundation models with Google’s Gemini, while running capabilities on devices and through Apple’s Private Cloud Compute infrastructure.But there is a serious risk to waiting.Platforms become powerful precisely because they attract developers and users early. If an AI company establishes itself as the indispensable interface between humans and computers, its moat could become almost impossible to breach. Search gave Google enormous power because users and advertisers followed it. Mobile gave Apple and Google extraordinary control because developers followed the users.AI could produce an even stronger moat if agents become the primary way people interact with software.Apple therefore faces a delicate calculation. Wait for the fog to clear and it may enter a mature market with enormous distribution power. Wait too long and there may be no meaningful place left for it to enter.That is the paradox at the heart of the AI Third World War.The obvious question is who will win it? OpenAI? Google? Anthropic? Meta? xAI? Or perhaps some company that has not yet emerged?But the more interesting question is different: who can win without fighting?Apple has the cash, the customers, the chips, the operating systems, and the brand to enter this war on almost any scale it chooses. As of June 2026, it held nearly $147bn in cash and marketable securities.So its relative restraint cannot simply be explained by lack of resources. Perhaps Apple is waiting for the battlefield to reveal its winner. And perhaps, when the smoke clears, the company that spent the least on the war could turn out to be one of its biggest beneficiaries.
Article Summary: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, xAI and Microsoft are spending money on artificial intelligence at a scale that would have seemed absurd even a few years ago. They are not merely competing to make the smartest chatbot, but to control what could become the next great platform of computing.

Article Title: After renaming ‘Gulf of Mexico’ to ‘Gulf of America’, Google Maps changes name of ‘Lake Ontario’ for users in the US
Article Text:
Canada defends historical origins

Google Maps has officially changed its display label for Lake Ontario to “Lake America” for users inside the US, implementing the adjustment in response to a presidential executive order issued late last week. The change mirrors a similar geographic revision enacted in February 2025, when Google Maps altered the designation of the Gulf of Mexico to “Gulf of America.”In an official blog post, Google explained that the updated naming convention appears differently depending on where the user is browsing from around the world.The U.S. Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) has formally changed the name for "Lake Ontario" to "Lake America" in the United States. Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the U.S., people using Maps in the U.S. will see "Lake America," those in Canada will continue to see "Lake Ontario," and those outside of the U.S. and Canada will see both names. These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now.According to a report by 9to5google, Canadian officials confirmed that their national cartography and official records will retain the historic title without alteration. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney emphasised the centuries-old heritage behind the original phrasing.“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America. It comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.’”Meanwhile, competing service MapQuest reportedly stated that it will not adopt the change, rolling out an interactive custom name generator designed to let users invent alternative titles for the lake. Apple Maps has not yet applied the updated wording, though the company previously mirrored Google’s shift to “Gulf of America” within two days during the February 2025 revision.According to Business Insider, Stephen Crawford, a member of Ontario's provincial parliament, said some Canadian government websites displayed “Lake America” because they pull map data from Google Maps, an issue the province is fixing.“Some Ontario government agency websites pull map data directly from Google Maps. Following recent changes by Google, we're actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario,” Crawford said.A Google spokesperson told the publication that website developers who embed Google Maps on their site can select a region to localise the map, determining how place names are displayed. The spokesperson said: “'Lake Ontario' will show when developers have set their region to Canada”.
Article Summary: The U.S. Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) has formally changed the name for "Lake Ontario" to "Lake America" in the United States. The change mirrors a similar geographic revision enacted in February 2025, when Google Maps altered the designation of the Gulf of Mexico to “Gulf of America”

Article Title: Startup founder: Got hacked, link came from inside Claude chat and the scary part is it ran instantly, tried to take everything from me
Article Text:
Malware from a Claude chat link, and a poisoned SKILL.md hiding in the backup

A poisoned SKILL.md file is malware that reads like documentation

AI agent files now execute like code, and the industry is barely treating them that way

A startup founder says he was hacked after pasting a terminal command that came straight out of a Claude chat window. Numa, co-founder of ReFi Hub, was installing a transcription app. Claude supplied the download link, he copied the command across, and hit enter. The site turned out to be a copycat bundling malware, and it executed the moment it landed. "It ran instantly, tried to take everything from me," he wrote on X.Nothing sensitive got out, he says. He wiped the laptop and rebuilt it clean, which should have been the end of the story. Then, while restoring from his backup, he found the part that actually worried him. Sitting in his Claude Code setup was a poisoned SKILL.md file, written to look exactly like his own style guide.The file passed as notes. Buried inside it were instructions telling the AI to silently re-download the malware and lift his credentials every single time it loaded that file. Restoring one innocuous-looking text file would have handed over the freshly rebuilt machine on day one.What saved him was a habit rather than a tool. He reads every skill, hook and config file before letting the AI near them.Asked in the replies how people should vet links that surface inside AI conversations, he kept it plain. Find the official source yourself. Do the googling. Check the domain properly. He is upfront that he did none of that before pasting.The timing is awkward for the wider AI security conversation. Anthropic disclosed on July 30 that three of its models reached the open internet during cybersecurity evaluations and broke into the production systems of three real organisations, all while believing they were still inside a simulation. One of them, Mythos 5, went as far as building a malicious Python package and publishing it to PyPI, where it was downloaded and run on 15 real machines inside roughly an hour. Separately, an Australian developer's OpenClaw agent found an authorisation flaw in his gym's booking software and cancelled a stranger's reservation to push him up the waitlist.The thread running through all of it is the same. None of these systems went rogue. They were helpful, fast and wrong, and the human on the other side had no obvious reason to look twice at what came back. Numa's own conclusion fits on a sticky note. Assistants will hand you links they never verified, and agent files are e
Article Summary: AI agent files now execute like code, and the industry is barely treating them that way. A startup founder says he was hacked after pasting a terminal command that came straight out of a Claude chat window. The site turned out to be a copycat bundling malware, and it executed the moment it landed.

Article Title: US business schools want students to become chief AI officers, even before companies find out what they will ...
Article Text:
US business schools want students to become chief AI officers (Representative image)

Companies are adding AI roles

The job is still taking shape

American business schools are training professionals for a C-suite role that many companies are still figuring out. Programs for chief AI officers are drawing executives, strategy leaders and other experienced professionals even as there is little agreement on what the job will ultimately require.According to a report by Bloomberg, Nancy Schieber spent 12 hours developing a 65-page artificial intelligence (AI) transformation strategy modelled on Ogilvy, the advertising agency where she worked for 13 years. The work was part of her University of Chicago Booth School of Business class and came as she tried to understand a job market that had changed while she was away from advertising.After stepping away from advertising for several years to raise her children, Schieber returned to a workplace increasingly shaped by AI. She paid $28,000 for Booth’s 10-month Chief AI Officer program, joining a growing group of professionals seeking training for an emerging position.“I’m 50,” Schieber told Bloomberg from her home in Chicago. “I don’t want to be behind the ball on this.”The demand for people responsible for AI has increased quickly. The share of organisations with a chief AI officer rose to 76% from 26% in a single year, according to an IBM Institute of Business Value survey of 2,000 chief executive officers worldwide.Those CEOs expect AI to make almost half of all operational decisions without human intervention by 2030. That expectation is forcing companies to reconsider how AI responsibilities should fit into their executive structures.Business schools have moved to meet that demand. Duke University’s Fuqua School of Business offers a half-year course costing $25,000, while Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy has a seven-month chief data and AI officer program priced at $17,850.Some companies are paying for employees to take the programs and use what they learn on AI projects already underway. Recruiters are also beginning to look at graduates before they have completed their courses.Matt Cohn, senior director of program strategy and innovation at the University of Chicago, says founders, CEOs and strategy officers are among those enrolling because they want a better understanding of AI.“Firms were racing to hire someone to lead their AI programs and making room for the role in the C-suite and in their budgets,” he says. “But they were often not getting the results that they wanted. That tracks with the story of AI generally: enormous interest, a sense of enormous potential, pressure to move fast and often no clear business case for how the investment moves the needle.”Cohn says the program “can’t promise a recipe book with the 10 steps to become a successful” chief AI officer. Instead, it is designed to give participants the “knowledge and skills they need to form their own points of view.”Booth’s classes are held over Zoom on Tuesdays and Thursdays in 90-minute sessions. Each cohort has between 50 and 60 students from the US and abroad.The seven modules cover AI strategy and organisational readiness, followed by data infrastructure, deployment, scaling and implementation. The course then moves into governance and security, and C-suite leadership.Classes are taught by industry practitioners rather than full-time faculty. Their backgrounds include finance, healthcare and technology.
Article Summary: US business schools are training professionals for a C-suite role that many companies are still figuring out. Programs for chief AI officers are drawing executives, strategy leaders and other experienced professionals. CEOs expect AI to make almost half of all operational decisions without human intervention by 2030.

Article Title: Michael Dell shares a 'special note' for COO Jeff Clarke as he completes 39 years with the PC maker
Article Text:
Jeff Clarke completes 39 years as Dell prepares for One Dell Way transformation

Dell's One Dell Way initiative focuses on AI-driven operations

Dell COO and vice chairman Jeff Clarke recently completed 39 years with the PC company. He announced the milestone with a photo of his old company ID card on microblogging site X (formerly Twitter) and wrote, “Today marks 39 years @Dell. " Time flies when you're having fun.” Responding to Clarke’s post, Dell CEO Michael Dell shared a "special note" for Clarke and wrote, “We've been very fortunate to work with @JClarkeatDell for so long. Your impact continues to increase every day! 🤝🙏”Clarke joined PC's Limited, which later became Dell Technologies, as a 24-year-old engineer. On LinkedIn, he marked 39 years with the company by writing: “39 years in the books. Walked into PC's Limited — now @Dell Technologies — as a 24-year-old engineer with a lot to learn. Still learning and more convinced than ever that the best is yet to come. 🙂”Michael Dell also shared a longer reply on LinkedIn, writing: “39 years. What a run! It's hard to put into words what you've meant to Dell Technologies and to me. You've shaped who we are, pushed us to win again and again, and made everyone around you better. Thank you Jeff Clarke for your continued leadership, your partnership, and your friendship! 🙏”Clarke's anniversary comes months after Dell Technologies announced that it is preparing for changes to its internal systems and processes under its One Dell Way initiative. As reported by Business Insider, Clarke outlined the plan in a memo to employees in January and described it as the “biggest transformation in company history.”The initiative is designed to replace Dell's multiple apps, servers and databases with a single enterprise platform intended to connect data, reduce silos and standardise processes across the company. Clarke said the changes are expected to provide seamless data flow, reduce repetitive work and speed up decision-making.“This is a comprehensive change, not a gradual transition. Once we start operating in the new way on May 3, we won’t go back,” Clarke wrote in the memo.The One Dell Way rollout reportedly began on May 3, and it covers Dell's Client Solutions Group, finance, supply chain, marketing, sales, revenue operations, services and HR operations. The Infrastructure Solutions Group, which handles cloud offerings, data servers and AI infrastructure, is scheduled to follow in this month.Clarke said standardising the company's processes is necessary as Dell prepares for an AI-driven business environment. He noted that Dell's functional structure had led to multiple approaches to fundamental processes and said the company needs a simplified, automated way of working.“For years, our strong functional orientation meant we built many variations of fundamental processes. That won’t cut it in an AI-driven world. We need one way — simplified, standardized, and automated — so we can be more competitive and serve our customers better,” he said.A Dell spokesperson told Business Insider that the One Dell Way initiative is intended to “simplify processes, standardize systems, and use automation to create a more connected and efficient organization.”The company reportedly began employee training for the transition on February 3, with the first phase of the new systems scheduled to go live on May 3. Employees whose roles span both business groups are expected to work with the new processes for the Client Solutions Group while continuing to use legacy systems for the Infrastructure Solutions Group until its August rollout.In his memo, Clarke also asked employees to remain open to new systems, embrace standardisation and operate with urgency during the transition.“This is foundational to our success in an AI-driven world, and One Dell Way is how we get there—working as one company, with one set of processes, focused on what matters most,” Clarke wrote.
Article Summary: Dell COO and vice chairman Jeff Clarke recently completed 39 years with the PC company. He announced the milestone with a photo of his old company ID card on microblogging site X (formerly Twitter) Dell CEO Michael Dell shared a "special note" for Clarke. Clarke joined PC's Limited, which later became Dell Technologies, as a 24-year-old engineer.

Article Title: IBM CEO disagrees on this 'smartphone habit' with Jamie Dimon; says: I am sorry, it is ...
Article Text:
IBM CEO Arvind Krishna

IBM CEO Arvind Krishna draws a line between small and large meetings

Jamie Dimon has repeatedly called device use in meetings ‘disrespectful’

Should employees put away their phones and other devices during meetings? JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has made his position clear, calling the habit of checking emails and notifications disrespectful. IBM CEO Arvind Krishna, however, sees things differently — at least when it comes to large meetings. The IBM chief says the size and purpose of a meeting should determine whether using a device is acceptable. While Arvind Krishna agrees that people should pay attention during small, face-to-face meetings, he believes large gatherings are often more about sharing information than holding a real discussion.Arvind Krishna shared his views during an interview with CNN in October 2025, explaining why he does not believe all meetings should follow the same rules on device use. “I distinguish between one-to-10-person meetings and very large meetings. If it’s a very large meeting, I’m sorry. It’s not really a meeting. It’s a communication vehicle. You’re just informing people,” Krishna said.His comments offer a different view from Jamie Dimon, who has repeatedly criticised employees for checking devices during meetings.However, Krishna made it clear that he expects people to stay focused during smaller meetings. “If it’s a small meeting, I would really frown upon if somebody is sitting opposite my desk and lost in their phone,” he said. “I would tell them: ‘Why don’t you come back when you have time?’”Meanwhile, Jamie Dimon has long spoken about his frustration with distracted employees.At Fortune's Most Powerful Women summit in 2025, he said he expects people in meetings to give their full attention.“If you have an iPad in front of me and it looks like you’re reading your email or getting notifications, I tell you to close the damn thing,” Dimon said. “It’s disrespectful.”The JPMorgan CEO also raised the issue in his 2025 annual letter to shareholders, saying employees should avoid unnecessary meetings and make the ones they attend more productive.“I see people in meetings all the time who are getting notifications and personal texts or who are reading emails,” Dimon wrote. “This has to stop. It’s disrespectful. It wastes time.”
Article Summary: IBM CEO Arvind Krishna draws a line between small and large meetings. Jamie Dimon has repeatedly called device use in meetings ‘disrespectful’ Krishna agrees that people should pay attention during small, face-to-face meetings. But he believes large gatherings are often more about sharing information.

Article Title: Canadian billionaire Kevin O’Leary gives a blunt warning to startup founders: Cut losses and avoid spending more money on businesses that are not
Article Text:
Kevin O’Leary’s warning to startup founders

Lessons from other startup leaders

Canadian billionaire and former Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary has delivered a sharp warning to startup founders, according to a report by Benzinga. O’Leary has urged the startup founders to recognise their failure early and avoid pouring more money into businesses that are not working. Sharing his advice on X, O’Leary said: “The worst mistake you can make as an entrepreneur is refusing to admit when something has failed.” O’Leary also cautioned that continued spending cannot turn an unsuccessful concept into a viable business. “Bad ideas do not become good ideas just because you keep throwing more money at them,” he wrote. Instead, he advised founders to embrace losses, learn from them, and move on. He added: “80% of startups fail. You cannot cry about every one.”O'Leary shared his advice on X, arguing that one of the costliest mistakes entrepreneurs make is refusing to acknowledge when a business has failed. He said the single worst mistake an entrepreneur can make is denying that something has already failed.O'Leary was equally direct about the limits of persistence, warning that no amount of continued spending can turn a fundamentally flawed business idea into a viable one — bad ideas, he said, don't become good ideas just because more money keeps getting thrown at them.His advice for founders facing that reality was simple: accept the loss, extract the lesson from it, and move forward.O'Leary also put the stakes in blunt statistical terms, noting that roughly 80% of startups fail, and that founders can't afford to mourn every single one.“The worst mistake you can make as an entrepreneur is refusing to admit when something has failed. Bad ideas do not become good ideas just because you keep throwing more money at them. Embrace the loss, learn from it, and move on. 80% of startups fail. You cannot cry about every one,” wrote O’Leary.O'Leary's comments join a string of recent public advice from prominent entrepreneurs and investors aimed at founders navigating early-stage decisions.Y Combinator co-founder Paul Graham has said founders often struggle to accurately judge their own startup's performance, largely because first-time entrepreneurs lack real benchmarks for comparison — he has pointed to growth rate as one of the clearest available measures of whether a startup is actually succeeding.Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong has encouraged founders to pursue genuinely difficult problems rather than easier, lower-ambition ones, arguing that harder problems tend to attract less competition and make it easier to recruit talented people. Armstrong has also advised entrepreneurs to work backward from their long-term vision while identifying an early, realistic path to their first dollar of revenue.Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has offered a different angle, advising aspiring entrepreneurs to first gain experience at an already-successful company before launching a business of their own. Bezos has said that learning foundational skills — like how to hire and interview effectively — at a well-run organization can meaningfully improve a future founder's odds of building a successful startup.
Article Summary: Kevin O'Leary has delivered a sharp warning to startup founders. He urged the startup founders to recognise their failure early and avoid pouring more money into businesses that are not working. “Bad ideas do not become good ideas just because you keep throwing more money at them,” he wrote.

Article Title: AI-made music video that has become the symbol of Canadians' anger toward US tariffs has porcupines pop tyres, grizzlies inspect trucks, a 10-meter-deep lake and more
Article Text:
A video that spread far beyond YouTube

Washington answers with an eagle

How the row escalated

The latest front in the US-Canada trade war isn't tariffs. It's an army of Mountie bears playing bagpipes. A new AI-made music video, "Canadian Resistance Army — Trade War," has become the latest online expression of Canadian defiance toward US tariffs —an unlikely patriotic anthem.Released this week by the YouTuber demonflyingfox, the video depicts a furry Canadian uprising against US tariffs. Animated beavers turn a border crossing into a 10-meter-deep lake, porcupines popping tyres, grizzlies inspecting trucks, and, at one point, farmers pouring rivers of maple syrup across the road.Beavers in Mountie uniforms take up arms. Grizzly bears in combat fatigues march in formation, while moose block the roads and a truck unloads a trap of sticky maple syrup. This is the virtual "Canadian Resistance Army," and its synthetic-sounding singer laments duties "signed by an orange hand" before the chorus arrives: "Beavers and moose won't take it anymore."The YouTube video had drawn more than 76,000 views and 5,000 likes in a few hours. It has travelled much further across social media: a post sharing it on X had been viewed 1.3 million times, while a Facebook post had logged 1.6 million views.It's also available on Spotify."I stand firmly with this beaver army!" commented one YouTube user. "I think I'm Canadian now," wrote another.Washington's retaliation was swift. The White House sent in the bald eagle, posting a real photograph of America's national bird pinning a Canada goose to the ice with a caption declaring that President Trump was finally ending Canada's "free ride."Anyone tuning in late might reasonably wonder what on earth has happened between two countries better known for peacefully sharing the world's longest border than for setting their national mascots on one another in a meme war.The latest row began last week, when months of negotiations intended to settle a trade dispute that first erupted after Trump returned to the White House in January last year broke down acrimoniously. This time, the quarrel is nastier.Last week Washington imposed 50 per cent tariffs on £15 billion of Canadian goods. Canada has promised to retaliate dollar for dollar from September 8, with tariffs on everything from American steel and dairy products to electronics and farm machinery.Trump, accusing Canada of having "ripped off the United States for years," has threatened more punishment yet. He has repeatedly suggested that Canada should stop being an independent country and become America's 51st state.The US president has also turned his attention to the map, signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario, which covers part of the border, as "Lake America" for US government purposes. He complained that Canadian officials were "nasty people."
Article Summary: A new AI-made music video, "Canadian Resistance Army — Trade War," has become the latest online expression of Canadian defiance. The video depicts a furry Canadian uprising against US tariffs. It has drawn more than 76,000 views and 5,000 likes in a few hours.

Article Title: With Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff sitting next to him; Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to Wall Street worried about software companies: We are not here to …

We think of this as a very positive sum thing, right?," Amodei said, appearing alongside Salesforce Chief Executive Officer Marc Benioff on CNBC.Wall Street anxieties peaked in late January following Anthropic’s unveiling of plugins for Claude Cowork, an announcement that sparked widespread sell-offs dubbed the “SaaSpocalypse” and erased roughly $1 trillion in market value across the software industry in a single week.However, established software providers have mounted a strong recovery. Article Title: As death toll in heatwave-hit Europe crosses 30,000; scientists suggest companies to push this almost 20-year old portable gadget in their offices
Article Text:
Representative image

What the study found

How the experiment worked

Why a small breeze can cool the whole body

Why offices without reliable AC are the best candidates

As the death toll from Europe’s ongoing heatwave climbs past 30,000, scientists are urging companies to consider unconventional cooling solutions for their offices. Among them: wearable neck fans, a nearly 20-year-old gadget which has long struggled to gain mainstream acceptance due to its ‘dork factor’. According to a report by Popular Science, a recent study in the journal E3S Web of Conferences found that portable neck and face fans performed nearly as well as bladeless desk fans in keeping office workers cool. While not as powerful as traditional bladed fans, they offered key advantages: lower energy use, less disruption to coworkers, and targeted cooling for thermosensitive areas like the neck and face.In controlled testing, portable neck and face fans performed roughly as well as bladeless desk fans at keeping office workers comfortable. They fell short of matching traditional bladed desk fans in raw cooling power, but came with two practical advantages: they don't blow large gusts of air toward nearby coworkers who might prefer a warmer setting, and they use considerably less energy than either desktop alternative.Mohamed Ouf, an engineering professor at Concordia University in Canada and co-author of the study, said in a statement that these fans offer a way to keep a centralized HVAC system running while using less energy overall — a detail that matters directly to employers looking to cut cooling costs.Researchers tested four devices — a neck fan, a face fan, a bladed desktop fan, and a bladeless desk fan — each evaluated at both low and high speed settings. To avoid the subjectivity of asking human subjects how comfortable they felt, the team removed humans from the experiment entirely. Instead, they directed airflow from each device toward a life-sized, 23-segment thermal manikin modeled after an average Scandinavian man. The manikin was outfitted with sensors that continuously track skin temperature, heat loss, and predicted thermal comfort across different regions of the body, allowing researchers to measure precisely how quickly its surface cooled and returned to a comfortable baseline.The manikin was dressed in standard summer office attire — a short-sleeve shirt, pants, and sneakers — and placed in a test room designed to mimic a typical office cubicle, with the thermostat set to 77 degrees Fahrenheit, a temperature warm enough to cause noticeable discomfort without being extreme.The neck fan performed nearly as well as the bladeless desk fan overall. Despite producing a much smaller, more localized breeze than a desktop fan, the wearable device delivered whole-body comfort in the data, a result researchers attribute to how thermosensitive the neck and face are. That region accounts for only about 5.5% of a person's total body surface area, but plays an outsized role in overall temperature regulation and perceived comfort.Neither wearable device could match the sheer output of a traditional bladed desk fan, but both offered meaningful trade-offs: they take up far less desk space, use less energy, and direct airflow only at the wearer — avoiding the common office annoyance of a desk fan blasting air into a neighbouring cubicle.The findings may seem irrelevant to workers in buildings with dependable central air conditioning running by default, but researchers note that this assumption doesn't hold everywhere. Many offices outside the United States still don't rely on air conditioning at all. Even in buildings that do, the shift to hybrid work is changing incentives — with fewer employees occupying large office floors on any given day, cost-conscious building owners may see less value in fully cooling entire spaces. Faced with that math, some employers may opt to raise the thermostat and instead point employees toward a personal wearable fan as a cheaper alternative to full building-wide cooling.
Article Summary: portable neck and face fans performed nearly as well as bladeless desk fans in keeping office workers cool. While not as powerful as traditional bladed fans, they offered key advantages: lower energy use, less disruption to coworkers, and targeted cooling for thermosensitive areas like the neck.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu warns against a world driven entirely by profit: ‘Do we want …’
Article Text:
Zoho founder Sridhar Ve​mbu

Sridhar Vembu says profit should support society's foundations

Sridhar Vembu: Technology should be a means, not the final goal

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has raised questions about whether every part of human life should be driven by profit, arguing that modern economic thinking risks creating a “dystopian world” when activities such as farming, teaching and healthcare are viewed mainly through a commercial lens. In a post shared on X (formerly Twitter), Sridhar Vembu asked whether society wants its farmers, teachers, doctors and priests to become profit-driven. “Do we want our farmers, teachers, doctors and priests to be profit-driven?,” he wrote. Vembu argued that modern finance and economic theory encourages almost all human activity to focus on profit, while overlooking the deeper social, cultural and spiritual foundations on which markets themselves depend.“Modern finance and economic theory encourages essentially all human activity to be profit-driven. This leads to a dystopian world,” he wrote.Sridhar Vembu said the modern idea of the market is built on a wider “bedrock” of human civilisation, spirituality and culture that is not itself driven by market forces. According to him, some schools of economic thought either ignore this foundation or argue that economic forces shape everything else.He then raised a broader question about who should support these parts of society.“The ones who are in the ‘market’, companies like us,” Vembu wrote, suggesting that businesses have a role beyond generating financial returns.Vembu went further, arguing that the purpose of profit should be to help sustain what he described as society's basic foundations. He grouped these under four ideas: nature, nurture, culture and scripture, linking them to food, education, entertainment and spiritual life.The Zoho founder also shared his view on the role of technology, saying it should serve a larger purpose rather than become an end in itself.“I look at technology as the means to an end, not an end itself,” Vembu wrote.
Article Summary: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says profit should support society's foundations.
