Article Title: How a Chinese company is using Blue Light to fight mosquitoes, claims 30 kills per second: Scans the area, locks on in 3 milliseconds and...
Article Text:
Blue laser fires, mosquito drops: Photon Matrix claims 30 kills a second

How the Photon Matrix laser mosquito killer finds a 2mm target in the dark

The blue laser mosquito zapper's safety case has no independent testing behind it

The mosquito laser is a 20-year-old idea that finally shipped

Mosquitoes kill roughly 700,000 people a year, which makes them the deadliest animal on the planet by a wide margin. Our defences have not changed much in a century: nets, coils, sprays, and a rolled-up newspaper. A startup in Changzhou, in eastern China, thinks the next step is a laser turret that sits on your patio and shoots the insects out of the air.Photon Matrix has opened preorders for its blue laser mosquito air defense system at $1,088, roughly Rs 95,000, after starting mass production in August. The company says the device locks onto a mosquito in three milliseconds and can take down up to 30 of them a second, in complete darkness, without chemicals and without noise. Those are the company's own numbers, and nobody outside the company has verified them yet.The unit scans a flat fan of light across the space in front of it and continuously measures how far away the background is. When something small crosses that plane, the distance reading changes. The system then checks the size, and if it matches a mosquito, between 2mm and 20mm moving slower than a metre per second, an internal galvo mirror points the laser down the same optical path the LiDAR just used and burns the wings.Coverage is a six-metre radius across a 90-degree arc, and a rotating base spins the device for something closer to full coverage. A companion app logs kills, plots a mosquito heat map, sets on-off schedules and, for reasons known only to the marketing team, ranks you on a global leaderboard.The obvious question about a laser strong enough to disable an insect is what happens when it misses. Photon Matrix's answer is a background check: the laser fires only when it detects a solid surface within range, and shuts off when it cannot find one. The company says the system has cleared certifications covering people, pets and birds, and that it ignores butterflies and other larger insects. It has also promised to publish more testing and safety data. Until an independent reviewer gets a unit on a table, buyers are taking that on trust, and the comment sections under every video of this thing are full of people asking about eyes.There are two versions. The outdoor blue laser model at $1,088 flashes visibly each time it fires. The indoor infrared model, at $988 or about Rs 87,000, uses a 976nm invisible beam pitched at bedrooms and hotel rooms. Both come with a rotating base, a 12-month warranty and a 20,000mAh power bank good for around four hours off mains. Delivery is quoted at roughly 120 days.The project raised $2.7 million on Indiegogo against a $20,000 target, with over 4,000 backers paying about $630 each, then slipped repeatedly on sensor calibration and safety approvals. The concept itself dates to 2006, when an astrophysicist who worked on Reagan-era missile defence pitched it at a brainstorming session. A prototype turret with a 50-metre range was demonstrated in 2010 and never found a buyer.So the century-old arsenal gets a new entry, and it works out to about a thousand dollars for the privilege of watching mosquitoes fall.
Article Summary: Photon Matrix claims its laser can take down 30 mosquitoes a second. It uses a LiDAR to measure distance and size of the target. The laser fires only when it detects a solid surface within range, and shuts off when it cannot find one.

Article Title: After 101-years, this California business is shutting down on August 31; owner says in an emotional note: Decision comes with ...
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation only

Why the 101 year shop is shutting down

What the note on shutting down says

Hank & Frank Bicycles Announces Retirement After 101 Years of Community Service

After more than a century of serving Bay Area riders, families, and adventurers, Hank & Frank Bicycles will officially retire and close its doors on August 31, 2026. This decision comes with full hearts, deep gratitude, and an enduring love for the community that has carried us for generations.

A Legacy Built on Trust

Founded in 1925, Hank & Frank has been a rare constant in a changing world—a 101-years legacy stewarded by only two families.

When Dale Dryer took over the business from Hank 57 years ago, he carried forward a tradition of craftsmanship, honesty, and neighborly care. Today, as we prepare to close this chapter, we reflect with gratitude on the generations of customers, employees, friends, and families who made this shop far more than a place to buy or service a bicycle.

Why This Shop Has Always Mattered

Our “why” has always been simple: to help people experience the freedom, confidence, connection, and joy that a bicycle can bring.

Whether it was a child’s first ride, a family’s weekend adventure, a commuter’s daily route, or a lifelong cyclist’s next great bike, we have believed that every rider deserves care, respect, and guidance they can trust.

We have had the privilege of watching children grow up on our bikes—then return years later to buy bikes for their own children. We have seen families ride through milestones, seasons, and lifetimes with us.

From our original home on East 14th Street in Oakland, through several locations over the decades, to our final and beloved home in the City of Lafayette for the past 52 years, every community we have served has shaped who we are.

With Deep Gratitude

To all of you—our riders, neighbors, friends, and extended family—thank you. Thank you for your trust, your stories, your friendly smiles, your loyalty, and your belief in what a local bike shop can mean to a community.

You invited us into your lives at birthdays, graduations, weekend rides, first commutes, race days, repairs, upgrades, and ordinary moments that became lasting memories.

Your support allowed us to do what we loved for more than a century: serve people well, stand behind our work, and help keep generations of riders rolling safely, happily, and confidently. That is a gift we will never take for granted.

Looking Ahead

As we look ahead, we also look forward to wishing Frank a joyful and well-earned next chapter.

At the same time, we are actively seeking the right person to carry on this extraordinary legacy, and we will keep our community informed as that search continues.

Between now and August 31, 2026, we invite you to stop by and be part of this final season with us:

* Pick out your next quality bicycle.

* Schedule service with our exceptional mechanics.

* Share a memory, a story, or a simple hello.

* Let us thank you in person for being part of our journey.

It has been our honor to help keep you moving for so many years. More than anything, we hope you know how deeply grateful we are—for every mile shared, every relationship built, and every moment of trust you placed in us.

With sincere gratitude,

The Hank & Frank Team

Hank & Frank Bicycles

After more than 101 years in business, a Bay Area institution is closing up shop. The century-old fixture of the Bay Area cycling community will permanently close its doors at the end of the month, marking the end of an era for one of the region's oldest bike retailers. Hank & Frank Bicycles, which first opened in 1925, announced that its final day of business will be August 31.The shop began operations on East 14th Street in Oakland before relocating several times, eventually establishing its permanent home in Lafayette, where it has operated for the past 52 years. The business changed hands 57 years ago when Dale Dryer took over from original founder Hank. His son, Frank Dryer, grew up sweeping the floors and assembling tricycles before purchasing the Lafayette storefront from his father in 1991.Unlike many recent legacy business closures driven by online competition or rising operational costs, the shutdown comes as the building changes hands. The property’s new owners plan to convert the space into a dance studio, prompting the younger Dryer to choose retirement rather than relocate. Dryer noted that while he is saddened to leave the community, the timing felt right, particularly without a successor to carry on the family trade.Customer loyalty remained steady throughout the decades, bolstered by a longstanding promise of free lifetime tune-ups with every bicycle purchase. To honor that commitment after the storefront closes, Dryer has arranged for a neighboring independent shop in Walnut Creek to take over the lifetime service perk for existing patrons.Patrons and longtime cyclists are visiting the Lafayette location in its final days to purchase bikes, schedule tune-ups, and share farewell notes with the staff before the shop closes its doors for good on August 31.
Article Summary: Hank & Frank Bicycles, which first opened in 1925, announced that its final day of business will August 31. The shop began operations on East 14th Street in Oakland before relocating several times. The business changed hands 57 years ago when Dale Dryer took over from original founder Hank Dryer.

Article Title: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman joins Elon Musk and Sundar Pichai in their Space data center plans; says: Let’s take our data centers to ...
Article Text:
​NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman joins Elon Musk and Sundar Pichai in their Space data center plans

A political liability on the ground

Not the first time Jared Isaacman has floated the idea

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has joined Elon Musk and Sundar Pichai in support of relocating data centers to Earth’s orbit. Along with the CEOs of SpaceX and Google, Isaacman is also pushing this idea to sidestep growing public anger over the facilities' environmental and economic toll in American communities. In an interview with Nexstar DC's Vinay Simot, Isaacman said: "Let's take our data centers, put them in Earth orbit, take advantage of that free fusion reactor that's out there for us and use that to ensure we do win the … space race for sure, but the AI race, too,"In January, at the World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, Elon Musk said that "the lowest-cost place to put AI will be in space, and that will be true within two years, maybe three at the latest," while Google CEO Sundar Pichai has said Alphabet is exploring "moonshot" concepts for data centers in space later this decade under an internal effort known as Project Suncatcher.Isaacman added that the move would "have immense benefits," as companies could leverage solar energy, which is the "free fusion reactor", to power data centers without straining terrestrial electric grids.Data centers, which fuel the growing AI industry, have quickly lost favour with the public with many saying their presence raises prices in communities and carries negative environmental impacts. Amid this pushback, US politicians are hastily trying to distance themselves from the facilities.Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, signed an order last week requiring that data center developers cover electricity costs and gain local backing for projects. Shapiro had previously boasted about these facilities' investments in his state.This is not the first time the NASA administrator has proposed the idea of sending data centers into space. In an early August appearance on the New York Post's "Pod Force One" podcast, Isaacman called the proposal a "fantastic" solution to the public's complaints."Elon [Musk] and others in the industry are like, 'Let's take the data centers that no one likes in your backyard — it seems like there's a lot of consensus on that — and put them into space where they won't bother anyone'," Isaacman said during the earlier podcast.He added that the space data centers would need solar panels "the size of several football fields.”
Article Summary: Jared Isaacman has joined Elon Musk and Sundar Pichai in support of relocating data centers to Earth’s orbit. Isaacman is also pushing this idea to sidestep growing public anger over the facilities' environmental and economic toll in American communities.

Apple smart glasses may use cameras to understand the real world

No display, but built-in speakers for music and calls

Apple could make its entry into the smart glasses market as early as next year, with a product focused on artificial intelligence rather than augmented reality. Article Title: Bill Gates, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang does not agree with you; says: I love Bill, but he is wrong as ...
Article Text:
Jensen Huang has previously suggested that skilled, blue-collar workers stand to gain significantly from the AI boom

Jensen Huang says he is open to some taxes, just not this one

A bid for reindustrialisation

Jensen Huang has pushed back on a proposal from Bill Gates to tax robots and AI tokens. The Nvidia CEO has argued that his own approach to sharing the wealth generated by the AI boom would look different from what the Microsoft co-founder has suggested. In an interview with Fox Business's The Claman Countdown, Huang said: "I love the heck out of Bill … but I don't see what he sees. I see something very, very different. And so my remedies will be a little different."This comes after Gates published an essay this week, titled "The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical." In it, Gates wrote: "Right now, if you're an employer and you hire someone, you pay payroll taxes on their earnings. But if you buy a robot, you can usually write it off right away as a business expense. The tax system nudges you toward replacing people with machines."Gates argued that this imbalance in the tax code could accelerate the pace at which companies replace workers with machines. This isn't Gates' first attempt to float the robot tax idea; he originally raised the concept in 2017, when economists broadly dismissed it as essentially a tax on productivity gains.Gates has suggested that governments will need the funds, reasoning that if AI takes over human jobs, state revenues from income tax will drop. "A tax would slow the rush away from human labour a little and raise money for retraining and a stronger safety net," Gates explained."I'm in favour of taxes. And I think that … for anybody who is productive, it's a great way for us to contribute back to society and the economy. But the fact of the matter is, there are probably lots of different ways to approach this,” Huang added.Huang's perspective is more positive. He said that while "of course" the nature of jobs would change, as it already has. "I believe … that this will be a net job creator. However, there are going to be many jobs will be disrupted, so we have to be sensible about that. We have to be sensitive about that and be supportive of that,” he added.While Gates suggests that companies could be incentivised to replace humans with robots because of existing fiscal policy, Huang says the historical precedent disagrees: "When companies are more productive, they don't lay off people, they hire more people. The reason for that is because companies have ambitions … and I would say the vast majority of the world's companies … have ambitions for growth. When they're more productive, when they're more profitable, [it] allows us to invest more and go after more growth. Nonetheless, overall, this is going to be a net job creator at a scale that we have never seen."Huang has previously suggested that skilled, blue-collar workers stand to gain significantly from the AI boom. Trades like plumbers and electricians, Huang has said, will be in high demand as data centers are built across the globe.Speaking this week, the 63-year-old tech titan suggested that the new economic era would be one of reindustrialisation.He explained: "We have lots and lots of white-collar workers, but we're also going to have a lot of skilled labour. And having a large population of skilled labour and people who build things and make things with their hands is tremendous for the United States. We want to reindustrialise the United States. We want to create more jobs. And all of that's going to happen right now as we speak with AI."
Article Summary: Jensen Huang has pushed back on a proposal from Bill Gates to tax robots and AI tokens. The Nvidia CEO has argued that his own approach to sharing the wealth generated by the AI boom would look different from what the Microsoft co-founder has suggested. This comes after Gates published an essay this week titled "The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical"

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang missing from Time's 100 most influential people in AI list for 2026
Article Text:
Jensen Huang, CEO, Nvidia.

Jensen Huang missing from Time 100 AI 2026 list

Elon Musk, Sam Altman and Dario Amodei appear in the list

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company has become one of the biggest suppliers of chips powering the artificial intelligence boom, has been left off Time magazine's 2026 list of the 100 most influential people in AI. The omission has drawn attention because Jensen Huang featured on the list in each of its first three editions, starting in 2023. The 2026 list includes several prominent figures from technology, business and entertainment, including Elon Musk , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.Time says its annual list recognises people who are shaping the key developments in artificial intelligence and influencing the technology's growth.Jensen Huang's absence stands out given Nvidia's central role in the AI industry. The company's graphics processing units, or GPUs, are widely used to train and run advanced AI systems, making Nvidia a major player in the rapid growth of the sector.Notably, Jensen Huang was included in Time's AI 100 lists in 2023, 2024 and 2025. However, he does not appear on the 2026 list.Time described the purpose of its list as identifying people who “best represent the year’s key storylines” and who are having the most influence on developments in AI.Several of the biggest names in AI are featured on this year's list. These include SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. The list also includes executives and leaders associated with companies including IBM, Google DeepMind, ByteDance, Broadcom, Databricks, Amazon and Oracle.Beyond technology leaders, the 2026 list also features names from entertainment and politics, including Ben Affleck, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Paris Hilton and US Senator Bernie Sanders.Time 100 AI list highlights changing influence in AITime's list is not a ranking of companies or a direct measure of business success. Instead, the publication selects people it believes have had significant influence on the major AI developments of the year. As a result, the list changes from year to year and can include researchers, business leaders, policymakers and public figures alongside technology executives.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang featured on the list in each of its first three editions, starting in 2023. The 2026 list includes several prominent figures from technology, business and entertainment. Elon Musk, Sam Altman and Dario Amodei appear in the list. The omission stands out given Nvidia's central role in the AI industry.

Subscription revenue continues to represent a vital pillar of Apple’s financial performance. This is due to the dact that the tech company posted $30.7 billion in Services revenue during its fiscal third quarter, reflecting a 12% year-over-year increase.Sequential gross margins across the services division dipped by more than 1%, driven by shifting product mixes and currency exchange fluctuations.The subscription price updates arrive as CEO Tim Cook prepares to step down on September 1. In announcing the leadership transition, Apple highlighted that expanding digital services had been a central strategic focus throughout Cook’s tenure.

Article Title: Elon Musk breaks silence on OpenAI cutting 3-year-old deal with Cursor over him; says: Sam Altman is …
Article Text:

‘Cursor was one of the very first users of OpenAI’

Here’s what OpenAI said on cutting off deal with Cursor

Elon Musk has responded after OpenAI said it is ending its partnership with Cursor, a coding tool recently acquired by Musk's SpaceX. The move ends a partnership that had been in place for around three years and adds a new chapter to the long-running dispute between Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. In an X (formerly Twitter) post, Musk appeared unfazed by the decision, saying he “couldn’t care less” and launching a fresh attack on Altman and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, calling them untrustworthy. “I couldn’t care less. Scam Altman and Greg Stockman are utterly untrustworthy assholes who stole an open source nonprofit,” Musk wrote in the post.Cursor was founded in 2022. It was recently acquired by Elon Musk’s space company SpaceX. Musk had sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman for "stealing a charity" by betraying the company's ​original nonprofit mission.“To work with a large partner like SpaceX, we typically rely on custom contracts to ensure compliance with our terms of service and that the integration provides for safety at scale. After Musk acquired Twitter, now part of SpaceX, the company broke⁠(opens in a new window) the terms of our contract (alongside many others).Under oath earlier this year, Musk admitted⁠(opens in a new window) that xAI, now also part of SpaceX, had violated OpenAI’s terms of service (terms which are similar to xAI’s own),” OpenAI said in an announcement.Reacting to the OpenAI announcement, Michael Truell, a co-founder of Cursor and now an executive at SpaceX shared an X post where he reiterated that Cursor was one of the very first users of OpenAI and that the space company is “speaking with the OpenAI team to resolve this”.“We’re sorry to see that OpenAI put out a note saying they plan to block Cursor users from accessing OpenAI models in three months,” Truell wrote in the post adding “OpenAI models serve about 5% of Cursor user traffic, and we’re speaking with the OpenAI team to resolve this”.“Cursor was one of the very first users of OpenAI, we’ve worked closely with their team for years, and we’ve trusted their platform to be neutral infrastructure for our business.”"Today, we notified SpaceX that we intend to wind down our contract providing OpenAI models to Cursor, with a proposed shutoff date of November 12, 2026. To maximize the time that developers can retain access to our models through Cursor, we are giving the maximum notice provided by our contract. This decision was incredibly tough, as we care deeply about our models being broadly available for developers. We are making this choice because we cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts.To work with a large partner like SpaceX, we typically rely on custom contracts to ensure compliance with our terms of service and that the integration provides for safety at scale. After Musk acquired Twitter, now part of SpaceX, the company broke⁠(opens in a new window) the terms of our contract (alongside many others). Under oath earlier this year, Musk admitted⁠(opens in a new window) that xAI, now also part of SpaceX, had violated OpenAI’s terms of service (terms which are similar to xAI’s own).Our custom agreement with Cursor gives us a limited time window to cancel it after a change of control. As AI capabilities advance, we also have a new level of accountability to ensure our upcoming model, Astra, is being used in accordance with our terms. Given all of this, we’ve decided to hold the contract cancellation to the latest date we can while not providing future models to Cursor.We’ve worked with Cursor for nearly four years and have enormous respect for their team, their product, and what they’ve built for the developer community. We know that the people most affected by this decision are the developers who rely on OpenAI models in Cursor. We care about their experience in this transition and we’re ready to go above and beyond to support them."

The move ends a partnership that had been in place for around three years and adds a new chapter to the long-running dispute between Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. In an X (formerly Twitter) post, Musk appeared unfazed by the decision, saying he “couldn’t care less” and launching a fresh attack on Altman and Open AI President Greg Brockman.

Companies placed on it can be barred from doing business with the US government and suffer reputational damage that can affect business relationships even outside the government arena.CXMT said the designation has already cost it.the company said in a statement to Reuters, adding that the lawsuit is meant to protect its business interests going forward.CXMT is China's top producer of dynamic random-access memory chips, or DRAM, a type of memory chip used widely in smartphones, personal computers, servers, and artificial intelligence systems. The company's revenue jumped 874% in the first half of the year, according to the Reuters report, and it has expressed hopes of eventually entering the US market.CXMT filed its complaint in the US District Court for the District of Columbia. The lawsuit names the Department of Defense, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg, and Assistant Secretary of Defense for Industrial Base Policy Michael Cadenazzi as defendants.The company said the Pentagon’s decision to designate it was “arbitrary,” not based on enough evidence, and violated its due-process rights. According to the complaint, CXMT provided information to the Pentagon for over a year to dispute the designation and get itself off the list.CXMT also pointed to a reversal earlier this year as evidence of inconsistent handling. The company said the Pentagon published a notice in February stating that CXMT would be removed from the list, then withdrew that notice the same day. CXMT alleges the Defense Department later relisted the company without adequately explaining the change.CXMT said in its complaint.CXMT's legal challenge follows a similar path taken by other major Chinese firms contesting their inclusion on the Pentagon's list. In June, Chinese technology and e-commerce giant Alibaba sued the US government over its own placement on the list.Precedent suggests such challenges can succeed. Smartphone and electric-vehicle maker Xiaomi filed a similar lawsuit in 2021 and was ultimately removed from the list.CXMT's case adds to a growing pattern of Chinese companies turning to US courts to contest national security-related designations, underscoring the tension between Washington's efforts to restrict China's access to advanced technology and Chinese firms' push to protect their standing in global markets, including their long-term ambitions in the US
